nodes.name: SOLID
nodes.description: Five object-oriented design principles, grouped under one acronym, for keeping code easy to change as it grows.
nodes.markdown:
SOLID is an acronym for five object-oriented design principles that aim to keep code changeable as it grows. Robert C. Martin gathered the principles, and Michael Feathers proposed the acronym.

| Letter | Principle                                                              | Rule                                               | Violation looks like                         |
| ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| S      | [Single responsibility](node:Single%20responsibility%20principle)      | A module answers to one group of stakeholders      | A billing change breaks a report             |
| O      | [Open-closed](node:Open-closed%20principle)                            | Add behaviour without editing stable code          | Each payment type edits the same `switch`    |
| L      | [Liskov substitution](node:Liskov%20substitution%20principle)          | Subtypes honour the parent's contract              | A subclass throws on an inherited method     |
| I      | [Interface segregation](node:Interface%20segregation%20principle)      | Clients depend only on the methods they use        | A test mocks twenty methods to use two       |
| D      | [Dependency inversion](node:Dependency%20inversion%20principle)        | Policy depends on [abstractions](node:Abstraction) | Business rules import the database driver    |

The principles address a common experience: a small feature request touches many unrelated files, and a fix in one place breaks something elsewhere. Each principle targets one source of that [coupling](node:Coupling), such as a class with too many jobs, a subclass that breaks its parent's contract, or a dependency that points toward a volatile detail.

The principles are heuristics, and applying them mechanically causes a different problem. An interface for every class, a file for every method and several layers of forwarding make a simple flow hard to follow. That outcome is a form of [premature abstraction](node:Premature%20abstraction). Apply a principle when the code shows the pressure it relieves. Two payment types do not need a plugin system, while a fifth might justify one. [YAGNI](node:YAGNI) and [KISS](node:KISS) act as counterweights.

SOLID was written with classes in mind, but most of it carries over to functions and modules in TypeScript. A function type can act as an interface, and a module boundary can hold a single responsibility. Substitution applies to anything with a contract, including an HTTP API whose new version must keep accepting old requests.
quotes: Should this new class get an interface so it follows SOLID?
Only if there's a second implementation or a test that needs one. Otherwise it's an extra file with no benefit.

nodes.name: Single responsibility principle
nodes.description: A module should have one reason to change, meaning it answers to one group of people with one kind of need.
nodes.markdown:
The single responsibility principle says a module should have one reason to change. Robert C. Martin, who named it as part of [SOLID](node:SOLID), later restated it as a module being responsible to one actor, meaning one group of stakeholders who request changes.

The principle is often misread as "a class should do one thing", which leads to many tiny classes. The actual test concerns who drives change. A class can have several methods and still satisfy the principle if one group's needs determine all of them.

The symptom is a change for one team breaking behaviour for another. Finance asks for a new overtime calculation, a developer edits the shared `regularHours()` helper, and an HR report that relied on the old figure changes without anyone noticing. Both groups' requirements meet in the same code, so unrelated work also produces merge conflicts.

```typescript
// Three actors, one class
class Employee {
  calculatePay() {} // finance
  reportHours() {} // HR
  save() {} // platform team
}
```

The usual fix is to split by actor into `PayCalculator`, `HoursReporter` and `EmployeeStore`, each working on shared employee data. A [facade](node:Facade%20pattern) can keep one entry point for callers that want it.

Splitting has a cost. Code that always changes together belongs together, and separating it creates [shotgun surgery](node:Shotgun%20surgery), where one change touches many files. Aim for high [cohesion](node:Cohesion): group what changes for the same reason and separate what changes for different reasons. At the other extreme, a class that keeps accumulating responsibilities becomes a [god object](node:God%20object).

Apply the principle when you see the pressure, such as two teams repeatedly editing one file. A small class with a single user does not need splitting because it could one day have two.
quotes: Why did the payroll fix change the numbers on the HR dashboard?
Both use the same hours method on `Employee`. That's two reasons to change in one class, so let's split it.

nodes.name: Open-closed principle
nodes.description: Software should be open to extension but closed to modification, so new behaviour does not require editing working code.
quotes: Every new payment provider means editing five `switch` statements.
We have four providers and more coming. Let's move them behind a `PaymentMethod` interface.

nodes.name: Liskov substitution principle
nodes.description: Any subtype must be usable wherever its parent type is expected, without surprising the code that relies on it.
quotes: Why is there an `instanceof ReadOnlyCache` check in the save path?
Its `set` throws, so it can't stand in for `Cache`. Give it a read-only interface and stop inheriting.

nodes.name: Interface segregation principle
nodes.description: Clients should not depend on methods they do not use, so large interfaces are split into smaller ones per client.
quotes: This test mocks the whole `UserStore` just to read one user.
The function only calls `findById`. Narrow its parameter to that and the test needs a one-line stub.

nodes.name: Dependency inversion principle
nodes.description: High-level policy and low-level details should both depend on abstractions, so business rules do not import infrastructure.
quotes: We can't test the discount logic without Postgres running.
It imports the client directly. Have the service define a small interface and pass the Postgres version in at startup.

nodes.name: DRY
nodes.description: Don't repeat yourself: each piece of knowledge should have one authoritative representation in a system.
nodes.markdown:
DRY stands for "don't repeat yourself". Andy Hunt and Dave Thomas defined it in _The Pragmatic Programmer_ (1999): "Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system."

The principle concerns knowledge rather than text. A tax rate, a validation rule or the definition of an active customer should live in one place. When it is duplicated, the symptom is a fix applied in three places out of four: the checkout shows one price, the invoice shows another, and nobody knows which is correct. The scattered edits that follow are known as [shotgun surgery](node:Shotgun%20surgery).

Code that looks the same is not always the same knowledge. Two functions may both check that a string is under 100 characters, one for a username and one for a product title. They match by coincidence and will change for different reasons. Merging them creates [coupling](node:Coupling) between unrelated features, and the shared helper gradually gains flags such as `isAdmin` or `skipValidation` as each caller's needs diverge.

| Duplication    | Example                                 | Action                |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| Same knowledge | Tax rate defined in two services        | Consolidate           |
| Coincidental   | Similar validation for unrelated fields | Leave it              |
| Unclear        | Two similar handlers                    | Wait for a third case |

The last row reflects a common rule of thumb called the rule of three: tolerate a second copy and extract on the third, when the shared shape is visible. Extracting sooner risks a [premature abstraction](node:Premature%20abstraction). Undoing a wrong abstraction usually costs more than removing duplication, because every caller has to be untangled.

DRY has a further cost across service or team boundaries. A shared library used by several services means a change can require coordinated releases, which can produce a [distributed monolith](node:Distributed%20monolith). Duplicating a small amount of code between independently deployed services is often the better trade-off.
quotes: These two handlers have the same ten lines. Should I extract a helper?
One's for refunds, one's for payouts, and finance keeps changing them separately. Leave them apart for now.

nodes.name: KISS
nodes.description: A design guideline to prefer the simplest solution that meets the requirement, because complexity has a lasting cost.
nodes.markdown:
KISS stands for "keep it simple, stupid", a guideline to choose the simplest design that meets the requirement. The phrase is commonly attributed to Lockheed engineer Kelly Johnson. In software, it means avoiding moving parts the problem does not require.

The symptom is a small task that takes days because of the structure around it. Adding a field to a form means editing a controller, a service, a mapper, two [data transfer objects](node:Data%20transfer%20object) and a factory, each of which only forwards the value. New team members need a diagram to follow a single request, and bugs appear in the handoffs between layers.

Complexity has a running cost. Everyone who reads, debugs or changes the code pays it, long after the person who added it has moved on. Simple code is easier to test, delete and replace.

Simple does not mean short. A clever one-liner can be harder to follow than five plain lines, and a single large script can be harder to maintain than two well-named modules. A useful test is how much a reader must hold in their head to make a correct change.

| Choice     | Simpler default         | Reach for more when                  |
| ---------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Storage    | One relational database | A measured load or data shape needs it |
| Deployment | A single deployable     | Team or scaling needs diverge        |
| Variation  | An `if` statement       | Several variants keep growing        |
| Reuse      | A plain function        | Several callers share real knowledge |

KISS can be misused to reject necessary work. Error handling, input validation and security are required complexity, and removing them makes a system shorter but not simpler. Distinguish essential complexity, which comes from the problem, from accidental complexity, which comes from the solution. KISS targets the second. It is closely related to [YAGNI](node:YAGNI), which is about not building for imagined future needs, whereas KISS concerns the shape of what you do build.
quotes: Do we need a queue and a worker for this nightly export?
It runs once a day and takes a minute. A cron job calling one function is enough.

nodes.name: YAGNI
nodes.description: You aren't gonna need it: do not build a capability until a real, current requirement calls for it.
nodes.markdown:
YAGNI stands for "you aren't gonna need it", a practice from Extreme Programming: do not build a capability until a current requirement calls for it.

The symptom is code that exists for a future that never arrived. A `StorageProvider` interface has one implementation, a config option has never been set to anything but its default, and a tenant column holds `1` in every row. Each of these still has to be read, tested and worked around, and later changes take longer because of them. The resulting smell is called [speculative generality](node:Speculative%20generality).

A speculative feature costs more than the time to build it:

| Cost        | What happens                                                  |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Build       | Time is taken from work with a known need                     |
| Delay       | Needed features ship later                                    |
| Carry       | Every later change must accommodate the extra code            |
| Wrong guess | The real need differs from the guess, so the code is reworked |

YAGNI depends on code being cheap to change later. Tests, clear module boundaries and regular refactoring are what make it safe to defer work. Without them, deferral turns into [technical debt](node:Technical%20debt) rather than saved effort.

The practice applies to features and speculative flexibility, not to basic quality. Error handling, tests and readable names are part of building the current requirement. Some decisions are also expensive to reverse, such as public API shapes, data formats, identifiers and security models, and those justify more thought up front. The idea of the [last responsible moment](node:Last%20responsible%20moment) helps here: delay a decision until the cost of waiting exceeds the cost of deciding.

A practical check is to ask what it would cost to add the capability when it is needed. If the cost is about the same as now, wait. If it would require migrating every customer's data, decide now.
quotes: Should we make the notifier pluggable in case we add SMS?
Nobody has asked for SMS. Call the email service directly, and extract an interface if SMS actually comes up.

nodes.name: Separation of concerns
nodes.description: Dividing a program so each part handles one distinct concern, such as presentation, business rules or persistence.
quotes: The nightly job has its own copy of the discount logic.
It's stuck inside the HTTP handler. Pull it out into a plain function and call it from both.

nodes.name: Composition over inheritance
nodes.description: Building behaviour by combining objects instead of extending classes, which avoids rigid and fragile class hierarchies.
quotes: We need an urgent version of `RetryingEmailNotification`.
That's a third level of subclass. Make retry and urgency wrappers around a `Channel` and combine them.

nodes.name: Law of Demeter
nodes.description: A guideline that a method should call only its close collaborators, not reach through them into objects further away.
nodes.markdown:
The Law of Demeter is a guideline that a method should only talk to its immediate collaborators. It came from the Demeter project at Northeastern University in the late 1980s and is often summarised as "only talk to your friends". A method may call methods on itself, its parameters, objects it creates and its own fields.

The symptom is a chain of property accesses that reaches through several objects, often called a train wreck:

```typescript
// Reaches through customer, wallet and card
order.customer.wallet.primaryCard.charge(total);

// Tells the order what should happen
order.chargeCustomer(total);
```

The first line depends on the shape of four objects. When `wallet` becomes optional or customers get several payment methods, every caller with that chain breaks, and the fix spreads across the codebase as [shotgun surgery](node:Shotgun%20surgery). Tests also suffer, because a mock has to return a mock that returns a mock.

Each reach adds [coupling](node:Coupling) to a structure the caller should not need to know about. Following the law moves behaviour to the object that owns the data, which is the same direction as [tell don't ask](node:Tell%20don't%20ask).

The law is not about counting dots:

| Code                                | Violation? | Why                                   |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `order.customer.wallet.primaryCard` | Yes        | Navigates another object's internals  |
| `items.filter(isPaid).map(toTotal)` | No         | Each call returns a new collection    |
| `query.where(a).orderBy(b)`         | No         | A fluent builder returns itself       |
| `dto.address.city`                  | Usually no | Plain data with no behaviour to hide  |

Applied rigidly, the law produces wrapper methods such as `order.getCustomerWalletCardLast4()` that only forward calls, and the outer class grows with every new need. If many such forwards accumulate, the data may be in the wrong place, or the caller may need a different object passed in directly. Passing `card` as a parameter is often simpler than adding a method to reach it.
quotes: Making `wallet` optional broke forty call sites.
They all reach through `customer.wallet.primaryCard`. Put a method on `Customer` so the path lives in one place.

nodes.name: Tell don't ask
nodes.description: A guideline to tell objects what to do instead of querying their state and making the decision for them outside.
quotes: Support found accounts with negative balances.
Three places check the balance and subtract on their own. Move it into `account.withdraw()` so the rule exists once.

nodes.name: Command-query separation
nodes.description: A method should either change state or return data, but not both, so reading a value never causes a side effect.
quotes: Adding a debug log changed the test results.
The log calls `getSession()`, and that refreshes the expiry. Split it into a read and an explicit `refreshSession()`.

nodes.name: Principle of least astonishment
nodes.description: A component should behave the way its users expect, so that names, defaults and results do not surprise them.
nodes.markdown:
The principle of least astonishment says a component should behave in the way most of its users expect. It applies to API design, naming, defaults, configuration and user interfaces. When behaviour and expectation differ, the design is usually the thing to change.

The symptom is a bug caused by a reasonable assumption. JavaScript's `sort()` compares values as strings by default, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` returns `[1, 10, 9]`. Application code produces the same kind of surprise:

| Surprise                                 | Expectation                    | Fix                       |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------- |
| `delete()` only archives                 | The record is gone             | Name it `archive()`       |
| `getUser()` writes to the database       | Reads have no effects          | Separate the write        |
| The default is to retry forever          | Calls eventually fail          | Use a bounded default     |
| One parser throws, another returns `null` | Errors work the same way      | Pick one convention       |
| A CLI flag deletes without confirmation  | Destructive actions ask first  | Require explicit consent  |

Expectation depends on the audience. The conventions of the language, framework and codebase set what users assume, so an API should follow them even where a different design might be slightly better in isolation. A method named `map` should behave like `map` everywhere else in that language.

Surprises cost the most at boundaries that are hard to change, such as a public API, a CLI or a library. After release, callers come to depend on the surprising behaviour, so correcting it becomes a breaking change. Review names and defaults before publishing them.

Apply the principle by making side effects visible in names, choosing safe defaults and staying consistent with neighbouring code. [Command-query separation](node:Command-query%20separation) removes one common source of surprise, and a shared [ubiquitous language](node:Ubiquitous%20language) reduces another by keeping names aligned with what the business means. Where unusual behaviour is necessary, document it at the point of use.
quotes: I called `user.delete()` and the row is still there.
It soft-deletes. That surprises everyone, so let's rename it `archive()` before more code depends on it.

nodes.name: Encapsulation
nodes.description: Bundling data with the operations on it and restricting outside access, so an object can protect its own rules.
quotes: How did this order get shipped with no address?
Four services set `status` directly. Make it private and add a `ship()` method that checks the address.

nodes.name: Information hiding
nodes.description: Designing modules so each one conceals a decision likely to change, keeping that decision out of other modules.
nodes.markdown:
Information hiding is the design practice of giving each module a decision that is likely to change and concealing that decision from all other modules. David Parnas introduced it in his 1972 paper "On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules". He argued that modules should be divided by what they hide, rather than by the steps in a processing flow.

The symptom of missing information hiding is a small technical change that spreads widely. Switching the date format, the cache key scheme or a database column means editing dozens of files, because each one learned the detail. When a storage change requires edits in the UI, the storage decision was not hidden.

The details worth hiding are those likely to change:

| Decision                    | Hidden behind                            |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Storage engine and schema   | A data access module                     |
| Third-party vendor          | An [adapter](node:Adapter%20pattern)     |
| Algorithm                   | A function or [strategy](node:Strategy%20pattern) |
| Data format on disk or wire | A serializer                             |
| Concurrency and caching     | A module's internal implementation       |

```typescript
// Leaks the decision: callers build the key
cache.get(`user:v2:${tenantId}:${userId}`);

// Hides it: the key format can change in one place
userCache.get(tenantId, userId);
```

Information hiding differs from [encapsulation](node:Encapsulation). Encapsulation is the language-level mechanism of restricting access, such as private fields. Information hiding is the design choice of what to conceal. A class can have only private fields and still leak a decision through a method like `getRedisKey()`, or through a return type that exposes a vendor's objects.

Hiding reduces [coupling](node:Coupling) and allows modules to be understood and changed independently. It is what makes a [deep module](node:Deep%20module) possible: a small interface in front of a lot of hidden behaviour. No interface hides everything, because some details show through as latency, failures or ordering, which is the problem described by [leaky abstraction](node:Leaky%20abstraction). Hiding also requires predicting what will change, so revise boundaries as actual changes show where the pressure is.
quotes: Why did renaming a cache key touch thirty files?
Every caller builds the key itself. Hide the format inside a `userCache` module.

nodes.name: Coupling
nodes.description: The degree to which one module depends on another, judged by how likely a change in one forces a change in the other.
nodes.markdown:
Coupling is the degree to which one module depends on another. Two modules are tightly coupled when a change in one is likely to require a change in the other, and loosely coupled when each can change independently. Larry Constantine developed the concept, and it was published with Edward Yourdon in _Structured Design_.

The symptom is a small change that spreads. Renaming a field breaks three services, one team's release waits on another team's, or a test fails in a module nobody touched.

The structured design scale lists these forms, from loosest to tightest:

| Form     | One module depends on                 | Example                         |
| -------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Data     | Only the values passed as parameters  | `tax(amount, rate)`             |
| Stamp    | A structure, using only part of it    | `tax(order)` reads one field    |
| Control  | A flag that steers the other's logic  | `render(data, isAdmin)`         |
| External | A shared format or protocol           | Two services parse the same file |
| Common   | Shared mutable global state           | A global `config` both modify   |
| Content  | Another module's internals            | Reading a private field         |

Coupling also exists outside the code. Temporal coupling means one service must be running for another to work. Deployment coupling means two components must be released together. A system split into services that must deploy together is a [distributed monolith](node:Distributed%20monolith), which keeps the coupling of a monolith and adds network failure.

Some coupling is required, because modules that share nothing cannot cooperate. The goal is to make it deliberate: depend on a narrow, stable interface rather than on internals, and keep things that change together in the same module, which raises [cohesion](node:Cohesion). Techniques include [information hiding](node:Information%20hiding) and the [dependency inversion principle](node:Dependency%20inversion%20principle). [Connascence](node:Connascence) gives a finer vocabulary for describing how two pieces of code are linked.

Removing coupling can go too far. Replacing a direct function call with an event bus hides the dependency without removing it and makes the flow harder to trace.
quotes: Why does a change to the user table need a release from the billing team?
Billing reads that table directly. They're coupled to our schema, so give them an API instead.

nodes.name: Cohesion
nodes.description: How closely the contents of a module belong together, judged by whether they serve one purpose and change for one reason.
nodes.markdown:
Cohesion is the degree to which the elements inside a module belong together. A highly cohesive module has one clear purpose, and its parts change for the same reasons. Like [coupling](node:Coupling), the term comes from Larry Constantine's structured design work. The two are usually discussed together, since modular design aims for high cohesion within modules and low coupling between them.

The symptom of low cohesion is a module you cannot describe without using "and", or a file named `utils.ts`, `helpers.ts` or `common.ts` that every other file imports. A change to one feature requires opening five folders, the files you open are mostly unrelated code, and unrelated work conflicts during merges.

The structured design scale ranks types of cohesion from weakest to strongest:

| Type            | Parts are grouped because       | Example                           |
| --------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Coincidental    | No real reason                  | `utils.ts`                        |
| Logical         | Same category of thing          | All validators in one file        |
| Temporal        | They run at the same time       | `startup()` does unrelated setup  |
| Procedural      | They run in sequence            | Steps in a long workflow function |
| Communicational | They use the same data          | Functions that all read a `Report` |
| Sequential      | One's output feeds the next     | Parse, then transform             |
| Functional      | They all contribute to one task | A `TaxCalculator`                 |

To raise cohesion, move code next to the code it changes with. [Package by feature](node:Package%20by%20feature) does this at the folder level, by placing a feature's routes, logic and queries together rather than scattering them across technical layers. At class level, the [single responsibility principle](node:Single%20responsibility%20principle) applies the same idea, and [feature envy](node:Feature%20envy) is a sign that a method sits in the wrong class.

Cohesion and file size are separate matters. A 600-line module that does one thing may be more cohesive than six 100-line files that must be read together, and splitting it can make things worse. Ask whether a typical change stays within the module. If it does, the boundary is working.
quotes: `utils.ts` is 2,000 lines and everyone conflicts in it.
Nothing in there is related. Move each helper next to the feature that uses it.

nodes.name: Connascence
nodes.description: A vocabulary for coupling, where two parts are connascent if changing one requires changing the other to stay correct.
nodes.markdown:
Connascence is a way of describing [coupling](node:Coupling) precisely: two pieces of code are connascent if changing one requires changing the other to keep the system correct. Meilir Page-Jones introduced the term in the 1990s. It names the kind of dependency, so a reviewer can say more than "these are too coupled".

The forms run from weaker to stronger:

| Form      | Visible | Both sides must agree on | Example                             |
| --------- | ------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| Name      | Static  | A name                   | A method name at a call site        |
| Type      | Static  | A type                   | A parameter type                    |
| Meaning   | Static  | What a value means       | `status === 3` means shipped        |
| Position  | Static  | An order                 | `createUser("Ada", true, false)`    |
| Algorithm | Static  | A computation            | Client and server hash the same way |
| Execution | Dynamic | The order of calls       | `connect()` before `send()`         |
| Timing    | Dynamic | When things happen       | A `sleep(100)` waiting for a job    |
| Value     | Dynamic | Related values           | Two copies of a price must match    |
| Identity  | Dynamic | The same instance        | Two modules must share one object   |

Static forms are visible in source code, while dynamic forms appear only at runtime and are harder to find. The symptom of a strong form is a bug with no compile error. Someone swaps two boolean arguments or changes what status `3` means, and the code still type-checks while behaving incorrectly.

```typescript
// Connascence of position
createUser("Ada", true, false);

// Connascence of name
createUser({ name: "Ada", isAdmin: true, sendInvite: false });
```

Three properties decide how much a given connascence matters: strength is how hard it is to detect and change, locality is how far apart the two pieces are, and degree is how many places are involved.

The practical guidance is to refactor strong forms into weaker ones, such as replacing a magic number with a named constant, which converts connascence of meaning into connascence of name. Connascence of algorithm is often the duplication that [DRY](node:DRY) targets. Keep the strong forms that remain close together, which also raises [cohesion](node:Cohesion). Two functions in one file that rely on call order are acceptable, while the same reliance across two services is a risk.
quotes: Why did swapping those two booleans compile but break signup?
That's connascence of position. Use a named options object and the compiler will catch it.

nodes.name: Abstraction
nodes.description: A simplified view of something that exposes what callers need and hides the details they do not need to know.
nodes.markdown:
An abstraction is a simplified view of something that keeps the details a user needs and leaves out the rest. A file is an abstraction over disk blocks, an HTTP client is one over sockets, and a `sendInvoice()` function is one over the steps needed to send an invoice. It lets a programmer work with a concept without thinking about how it is implemented.

Abstraction and [information hiding](node:Information%20hiding) are related but distinct. Abstraction concerns what a caller sees and thinks about. Information hiding concerns which design decisions are kept out of reach. A good interface does both.

Abstractions come in different forms:

| Form                 | Hides                     | Example                    |
| -------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Function             | Steps of a computation    | `calculateTax(order)`      |
| Data type            | Representation            | `Money` instead of a float |
| Interface            | Which implementation runs | `PaymentGateway`           |
| Module               | Internal structure        | A `billing` package        |
| Protocol or platform | The machinery beneath     | SQL, HTTP, a filesystem    |

A useful abstraction reduces what the reader must know. A poor one adds a name without removing any detail, so the reader has to open it anyway. The symptom is a wrapper whose methods pass through to one call, or a helper such as `fetchData(url, true, false, "legacy")`, where each flag exists because a caller needed something different. A [deep module](node:Deep%20module) is the favourable shape: a small interface over substantial behaviour.

Abstractions are usually more useful when drawn from several working examples, because the examples show what actually varies. Introduced too early, they encode a guess, which is [premature abstraction](node:Premature%20abstraction), and later requirements get forced into the wrong shape. Keeping some duplication until the pattern is clear is often cheaper than untangling the wrong design, a trade-off discussed under [DRY](node:DRY).

No abstraction is complete. Details such as latency or failure can show through, as described under [leaky abstraction](node:Leaky%20abstraction).
quotes: This `fetchData` helper has five boolean flags now.
Each caller wanted something different. Inline it and see what the calls actually have in common.

nodes.name: Leaky abstraction
nodes.description: An abstraction whose hidden details show through, forcing its users to understand the layer it was meant to hide.
nodes.markdown:
A leaky [abstraction](node:Abstraction) is one whose hidden details affect the people using it, so they have to understand the layer underneath anyway. Joel Spolsky popularised the term in his 2002 essay "The Law of Leaky Abstractions", which argued that all non-trivial abstractions leak to some degree.

The symptom is code that works until it meets a condition the interface did not mention. An ORM using [lazy loading](node:Lazy%20load) makes a list page look like ordinary object access, then the page takes eight seconds because each `order.customer` runs a query. A remote call looks like a local function until the network times out.

| Abstraction           | What it hides        | How it leaks                         |
| --------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| ORM                   | SQL and query plans  | N+1 queries, missing indexes         |
| Remote procedure call | The network          | Timeouts, partial failure, retries   |
| Filesystem            | Disks and mounts     | Slow or failed writes on network drives |
| Garbage collection    | Memory management    | Pauses, leaks through held references |
| `async`/`await`       | Concurrency          | Interleaving between awaits          |
| Object storage folders | A flat key space    | A rename is a copy and a delete      |

Some leaks come from design choices and can be avoided. A data access method that returns a query builder, a service that throws `PrismaClientKnownRequestError`, or a domain type with a `_id` field passes an implementation detail to callers. Return domain types, translate errors at the boundary, and use an [adapter](node:Adapter%20pattern) or [anti-corruption layer](node:Anti-corruption%20layer) around external systems.

Other leaks cannot be removed, because latency, failure and resource limits come from the hardware and network. For those, make the cost visible in the interface: return a `Promise`, accept a timeout, and offer batch operations. Presenting a network call as a plain getter hides information callers need.

Teams should know one level below the abstractions they rely on, such as SQL for ORM users and TCP basics for anyone calling HTTP services. The abstraction saves time in normal operation, and that knowledge is needed when it fails.
quotes: The orders page got slow, but the code is just a loop over `order.customer`.
That property runs a query each time. The ORM is leaking, so load customers in one batch.

nodes.name: Deep module
nodes.description: A module with a small interface hiding a large amount of functionality, so callers get much behaviour for little knowledge.
quotes: To send an email I have to build a transport, a template and a retry policy first.
That module is shallow. Give it one `send(to, template, data)` and keep the rest inside.

nodes.name: Seam
nodes.description: A place where behaviour can be changed without editing the code at that place, often used to test legacy code.
quotes: I can't test renewals without hitting Stripe.
Add a seam. Pass the billing client in as a parameter and give the test a fake.

nodes.name: Inversion of control
nodes.description: A design where a framework or caller decides when your code runs, instead of your code directing the whole flow.
quotes: Where is this handler called from? I can't find a call site.
There isn't one. The framework invokes it through the route registration, so start there.

nodes.name: Service locator
nodes.description: A central registry that code asks for its dependencies at runtime, which hides what each class actually needs.
quotes: This test crashes with 'mailer not registered', but the class doesn't mention a mailer.
It pulls one from the service locator. Pass the mailer to the constructor so the dependency is visible.

nodes.name: Circular dependency
nodes.description: Two or more modules that depend on each other directly or indirectly, so none can be loaded or understood alone.
quotes: Tests crash with 'Class extends value undefined', but only when run alone.
That's an import cycle between `order` and `customer`. Move the shared base class into its own module.

nodes.name: Stable dependencies principle
nodes.description: Packages should depend in the direction of stability, so code that is hard to change never relies on code that changes often.
nodes.markdown:
The stable dependencies principle says a package should only depend on packages that are more stable than itself. Robert C. Martin defined it as one of his package design principles. "Stable" here means hard to change because many other packages depend on it. It does not mean unchanging.

The symptom is a small edit to a volatile package forcing a large rebuild and retest. A shared `common` package imports a feature package for one helper. Every change to that feature now rebuilds everything that uses `common`, and a minor UI tweak can hold up other teams' releases.

Martin measures this with an instability metric, `I = Ce / (Ca + Ce)`. Ca, or afferent [coupling](node:Coupling), counts the packages that depend on this one. Ce, or efferent coupling, counts the packages this one depends on. The result runs from 0, stable, to 1, unstable.

| Package        | Ca  | Ce  | I    | Role                                |
| -------------- | --- | --- | ---- | ----------------------------------- |
| `domain-types` | 8   | 0   | 0.00 | Many depend on it, so it changes rarely |
| `billing`      | 2   | 3   | 0.60 | Sits in the middle                  |
| `admin-ui`     | 0   | 5   | 1.00 | Free to change                      |

The rule requires I to decrease along each dependency arrow, as in `admin-ui` to `billing` to `domain-types`.

A stable package is hard to change, so it should not contain things that need frequent change. Martin's companion rule, the stable abstractions principle, says stable packages should be abstract, so they can be extended without being modified, in line with the [open-closed principle](node:Open-closed%20principle). When a stable package needs something from a volatile one, apply the [dependency inversion principle](node:Dependency%20inversion%20principle): define an interface in the stable package and implement it in the volatile one.

The metric is a guide. It counts dependencies without weighing them, and a concrete date library can sit at I = 0 without problems because it rarely changes. Use the numbers to find a widely used package that depends on a fast-changing one.
quotes: Why does a copy change in the admin UI rebuild everything?
`common` imports from `admin-ui`. That arrow points at something less stable, so move the helper down.

nodes.name: Acyclic dependencies principle
nodes.description: The dependency graph between packages must contain no cycles, so each package can be built, tested and released separately.
nodes.markdown:
The acyclic dependencies principle says the dependency graph between packages must have no cycles. Robert C. Martin defined it among his package design principles. Following dependencies from any package should never lead back to where you started, which makes the graph a directed acyclic graph.

It addresses what Martin called the "morning after syndrome". A developer's code worked yesterday, but today it fails because someone changed a package it depends on. Teams respond by coordinating releases, and when packages depend on one another in a loop, none can be released without the others. A [circular dependency](node:Circular%20dependency) turns those packages into one large unit for building, testing and versioning, even though they live in separate directories.

| Graph   | Build order                      | Effect of a change                 |
| ------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Acyclic | A clear order from the leaves up | Affects only dependents            |
| Cyclic  | No valid order                   | Affects every package in the cycle |

```text
Before:  billing -> orders -> customers -> billing

After:   billing -> orders -> customers -> billing-api
         billing -> billing-api
```

Two standard techniques break a cycle. The first is the [dependency inversion principle](node:Dependency%20inversion%20principle): one package depends on an interface, and the other implements it, as `billing` implements `billing-api` above. The second is to extract the code both packages use into a new package that they both depend on. If the packages are really one concept, merging them is also an option.

Cycles are easier to prevent than to remove. They usually arrive through one small convenience import during ordinary work, so enforce the rule with a dependency check in CI, which acts as a [fitness function](node:Fitness%20function). Once several cycles have formed, separating them takes planned effort, and the codebase drifts toward a [big ball of mud](node:Big%20ball%20of%20mud).

The principle pairs with the [stable dependencies principle](node:Stable%20dependencies%20principle), which governs the direction the arrows should point. Cycles inside a single package are a smaller concern because the package is released as a unit, though they can still cause load-order errors.
quotes: Why can't we release `orders` without also releasing `billing`?
They depend on each other through `customers`. Extract a `billing-api` package to break the cycle.

nodes.name: Package by feature
nodes.description: Organising code into folders by business capability, instead of by technical layer such as controllers and services.
nodes.markdown:
Package by feature is a way of organising source code so that top-level folders represent business capabilities, such as `orders` or `billing`, instead of technical layers such as `controllers` or `services`. Everything one feature needs sits together.

The symptom of the alternative, package by layer, is that a single feature change touches a file in every folder. Adding a field to an order means jumping between `controllers/`, `services/`, `repositories/`, `dtos/` and `validators/`, each holding dozens of unrelated files. The folder tree describes the framework rather than what the application does.

```text
# Package by layer          # Package by feature
src/                        src/
  controllers/                orders/
    orders.ts                   routes.ts
    billing.ts                  place-order.ts
  services/                     order-store.ts
    orders.ts                   index.ts
    billing.ts                billing/
  repositories/                 routes.ts
    orders.ts                   invoice.ts
    billing.ts                  index.ts
```

|                     | By layer                   | By feature                     |
| ------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Typical change      | Touches many folders       | Stays in one folder            |
| [Cohesion](node:Cohesion) | Low, grouped by file type | High, grouped by purpose  |
| Removing a feature  | Search across the tree     | Delete a folder                |
| Team ownership      | Shared across layers       | One team can own a folder      |
| Technical patterns  | Easy to see in one place   | Need shared conventions        |

Folders alone do not create a boundary. Without enforcement, `billing` can import a private file in `orders`, and the features become [coupled](node:Coupling). Give each feature a public entry point such as `index.ts`, and enforce it with import rules or a tool such as `dependency-cruiser`. Calls between features then go through that interface or through events.

Not everything belongs to a feature. Logging, database connections and design system components go in a small shared area, which should stay free of business logic so it does not become a dumping ground. Layers can still exist inside a feature that is large enough to need them, and small projects can stay flat.

This structure is the folder-level form of [vertical slice architecture](node:Vertical%20slice%20architecture). It also makes a later move to a modular monolith or a separate service easier, because the boundaries already exist. Feature folders can also match team boundaries, the alignment described by [Conway's law](node:Conway's%20law).
quotes: Adding a coupon field meant editing seven folders.
We're organised by layer. Let's move coupon code into a `coupons` feature folder, behind one `index.ts`.

nodes.name: Factory method
nodes.description: Defining a method that creates an object so subclasses decide which concrete class is produced.
quotes: Adding PayPal means editing the provider switch in nine places.
Move it into one `createPaymentClient` factory and have the nine call sites use that.

nodes.name: Abstract factory
nodes.description: An interface for creating families of related objects so code gets a matching set without naming concrete classes.
quotes: Staging wrote to the local disk but queued jobs on real SQS.
Those were picked by separate flags. Use one environment factory so they can't diverge.

nodes.name: Builder pattern
nodes.description: Constructing a complex object step by step through a separate builder, then producing it with a final call.
quotes: Why did forty tests break when we added a required field to `Order`?
Every test constructs it by hand. Add an order builder with valid defaults and only override what each test needs.

nodes.name: Prototype pattern
nodes.description: Creating new objects by copying an existing instance instead of constructing them from scratch.
quotes: Duplicating a dashboard and editing it changes the original as well.
The clone is shallow, so both share the same widgets array. Copy the nested state in `clone()`.

nodes.name: Singleton
nodes.description: A class restricted to one instance with a global access point, useful for shared resources but easy to overuse.
quotes: This test only fails when the full suite runs.
An earlier test changed the `Config` singleton. Inject the config so each test gets its own.

nodes.name: Object pool
nodes.description: Reusing a fixed set of expensive objects by borrowing and returning them instead of creating and destroying each one.
quotes: The API is hanging, but the database is nearly idle.
Check the pool. The error path in checkout never releases its connection, so we've run out.

nodes.name: Adapter pattern
nodes.description: A wrapper that converts one interface into the interface a caller expects, so incompatible code can work together.
quotes: Upgrading the Stripe SDK broke forty files.
Its types are used everywhere. Put it behind a `PaymentGateway` adapter so the next upgrade touches one class.

nodes.name: Bridge pattern
nodes.description: Splitting an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently through composition.
quotes: Adding WhatsApp means writing a new class for all eight notification types.
Channel and message type are separate dimensions. Bridge them so WhatsApp is one sender class.

nodes.name: Composite pattern
nodes.description: Treating individual objects and groups of objects through one interface by arranging them in a tree.
quotes: Permissions work for nested groups until someone adds a group inside a group inside a group.
The check only recurses twice. Model groups as a composite so any depth works.

nodes.name: Decorator pattern
nodes.description: Wrapping an object with another that has the same interface to add behaviour without changing the original class.
quotes: Our request metrics dropped by half after the caching release.
The logging decorator is now inside the cache, so hits aren't counted. Move it to the outside.

nodes.name: Facade pattern
nodes.description: A single, simpler interface over a complicated subsystem, so callers do not need to coordinate its parts.
quotes: The admin tool created an order without reserving stock.
It calls the services by hand. Route it through the checkout facade like the API does.

nodes.name: Flyweight pattern
nodes.description: Saving memory by sharing the immutable parts of many similar objects and passing the varying parts in at use.
quotes: The map tab dies at around 200,000 markers.
Each marker holds its own copy of the icon bitmap. Share one flyweight per icon type and store only positions.

nodes.name: Proxy pattern
nodes.description: A stand-in object with the same interface as another, controlling when and how the real object is accessed.
quotes: This endpoint runs 400 queries to render a list of 400 orders.
`order.customer` is a lazy proxy. Eager-load customers in the original query.

nodes.name: Chain of responsibility
nodes.description: Passing a request along a sequence of handlers, where each one can handle it, forward it or stop it.
quotes: Requests to the upload route hang with no error.
The new quota middleware never calls `next` when the user is under the limit.

nodes.name: Command pattern
nodes.description: Representing a request as an object so it can be queued, logged, retried or undone.
quotes: Undo only works for about half of the editor's actions.
The rest mutate state in their click handlers. Move them to commands with an `undo` method.

nodes.name: Interpreter pattern
nodes.description: Representing a small language's grammar as classes so that expressions in that language can be evaluated.
quotes: Our discount rules JSON has grown nested `or` blocks and nobody can tell how they evaluate.
It's a language now. Define the node types and write a small interpreter instead of more special cases.

nodes.name: Iterator pattern
nodes.description: Providing a standard way to traverse a collection one element at a time without exposing its internal structure.
quotes: The export job gets OOM-killed now that we have two million rows.
It loads them all first. Iterate with a cursor and write one batch at a time.

nodes.name: Mediator pattern
nodes.description: Routing communication between objects through one coordinator so they do not refer to each other directly.
quotes: Changing the country picker broke the coupon field again.
They all call each other. Have the form mediate, so each field only reports that it changed.

nodes.name: Memento pattern
nodes.description: Capturing an object's state in an opaque snapshot so it can be restored later without exposing its internals.
quotes: Undo restores the title but leaves the edited table cells.
The snapshot holds a reference to the cells array. Deep-copy it when saving the memento.

nodes.name: Observer pattern
nodes.description: Letting objects subscribe to a subject and be notified automatically whenever its state changes.
quotes: Memory climbs every time someone opens and closes the chat panel.
The panel subscribes on mount and never unsubscribes. Return a cleanup function from the effect.

nodes.name: State pattern
nodes.description: Moving state-specific behaviour into separate objects so an object changes how it acts when its state changes.
quotes: A cancelled order got shipped because `ship()` didn't check for the new status.
Status checks are scattered across every method. Model the lifecycle as explicit states so illegal transitions fail.

nodes.name: Strategy pattern
nodes.description: Defining interchangeable algorithms behind one interface so the one in use can be selected at runtime.
quotes: Every new promotion means another branch in `calculatePrice`, and last week's broke member pricing.
Make each pricing rule a strategy and select it from a lookup table.

nodes.name: Template method
nodes.description: A base class method that fixes an algorithm's steps while subclasses override selected steps.
quotes: We fixed the date validation, but XML imports still accept bad dates.
XML has its own copy of the flow. Move the shared steps into one template and override only parsing.

nodes.name: Visitor pattern
nodes.description: Adding new operations to a set of classes by placing them in separate visitor objects instead of editing each class.
quotes: We added a new AST node and the formatter silently dropped it.
The formatter uses `instanceof` checks. Make it a visitor so a new node type is a compile error.

nodes.name: Null object pattern
nodes.description: Replacing a null reference with an object that has the same interface and deliberately does nothing.
quotes: Orders were marked paid all weekend with no charges in Stripe.
The missing key fell back to `NullPaymentGateway`. Payments must fail at startup instead of doing nothing.

nodes.name: Transaction script
nodes.description: Organising business logic as one procedure per request, each handling its own validation, rules and persistence.
quotes: Cancelling from the admin panel still refunds shipped orders.
The check only exists in the customer-facing script. Move it onto `Order` so both paths use it.

nodes.name: Domain model
nodes.description: An object model of a business in which data and behaviour live together and the objects enforce the rules.
quotes: Where does the rule for cancelling an order live?
In four handlers. Move it onto `Order` so there is one version to change.

nodes.name: Service layer
nodes.description: An application boundary that exposes use cases and coordinates transactions, domain objects and infrastructure.
quotes: The CLI refund skips the fraud check that the API runs.
Each has its own copy. Move refunds into the service layer and have both call it.

nodes.name: Active record
nodes.description: An object that wraps a database row and carries both its domain logic and its own persistence methods.
quotes: Why did the backfill email every customer?
`User` has an `afterSave` hook that sends the notification. Run the backfill with callbacks skipped, then move that email into the signup use case.

nodes.name: Data mapper
nodes.description: A layer that moves data between objects and a database while keeping each unaware of the other.
quotes: Renaming `cust_ref` touched thirty files.
Those files read row fields directly. Put a data mapper in front of the table so the next rename lives in one place.

nodes.name: Unit of work
nodes.description: An object that tracks changes during a business operation and writes them to the database as one commit.
quotes: We have paid orders with no ledger entries.
Each repository commits separately. Wrap the payment in one unit of work so both writes succeed or fail together.

nodes.name: Identity map
nodes.description: A per-session registry that ensures each database row is loaded into exactly one in-memory object.
quotes: The test updates the row with raw SQL, but `findById` still returns the old status.
The session's identity map is handing back the loaded instance. Refresh it or read through a new session.

nodes.name: Lazy load
nodes.description: Deferring the loading of related data until code first accesses it, at the risk of hidden N+1 queries.
quotes: The orders page makes 340 queries.
Each row lazily loads its customer. Fetch the customers in one batch with the list query.

nodes.name: Data transfer object
nodes.description: A plain object with no business logic that carries data across a boundary such as an API or layer.
quotes: Why is `passwordHash` in the profile response?
The handler serialises the user row. Return a `UserResponse` DTO that lists only the public fields.

nodes.name: Gateway pattern
nodes.description: An object that wraps access to an external system behind an interface owned by the application.
quotes: Upgrading the Stripe SDK changed 38 files.
Every feature calls it directly. Add a `PaymentGateway` and move the SDK behind it as part of this upgrade.

nodes.name: Specification pattern
nodes.description: Representing a business rule as a combinable object that answers whether a candidate satisfies it.
quotes: The button says the customer can reorder, but checkout rejects them.
The UI and checkout each have their own rule. Define `canReorder` once and have both call it.

nodes.name: Plugin architecture
nodes.description: A structure where a host application defines extension points and separately packaged modules add behaviour.
quotes: Another customer wants a custom export format.
Stop adding branches to the exporter. Define an export hook and ship this format as a plugin.

nodes.name: Front controller
nodes.description: A single handler that receives every web request, runs shared processing and dispatches to route-specific code.
quotes: The new reports endpoint was reachable without logging in.
Auth is applied per route. Move it into the front controller and make public routes opt out.

nodes.name: Model-view-controller
nodes.description: A user interface pattern dividing code into a model for data, a view for display and a controller for input.
quotes: The checkout action is 400 lines, and the mobile API has a copy of it.
Extract the logic into a service so both controllers only handle input and output.

nodes.name: Model-view-presenter
nodes.description: A UI pattern where a presenter holds presentation logic and updates a passive view through an interface.
quotes: Testing the login error means booting an emulator.
Move the logic to a presenter behind a `LoginView` interface, then test it with a fake view.

nodes.name: Model-view-viewmodel
nodes.description: A UI pattern where a viewmodel exposes state and commands and the view binds to them declaratively.
quotes: The cart total stays stale after removing an item.
Someone set it by hand in the click handler. Make it a computed value on the viewmodel.

nodes.name: Ubiquitous language
nodes.description: A shared vocabulary that developers and domain experts use in conversation, documents and code.
nodes.markdown:
A ubiquitous language is a shared vocabulary that developers and domain experts use for a business domain, in conversation, in documents and in the code itself. Eric Evans introduced the term in Domain-Driven Design (2003). If the business says a policy is "renewed", the code has a `renew()` method and not `updateStatus(3)`.

The practice addresses translation between business and engineering. When sales says "account" for a company, support says "account" for a login, and the code calls both `User`, every conversation needs interpretation, and a ticket can be built correctly against the wrong meaning. The mismatch is often found late, when a feature ships and the stakeholder says it is not what they asked for.

| Business says       | Code without a shared language | Code with one             |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------- |
| Renew a policy      | `updateStatus(policy, 3)`      | `policy.renew()`          |
| Member has lapsed   | `user.flag === false`          | `member.hasLapsed()`      |
| Item is back-ordered | `item.qty < 0`                | `item.isBackOrdered()`    |

A ubiquitous language applies within one bounded context and is not a company-wide glossary. "Customer" can legitimately mean different things in billing and in shipping, and forcing one definition produces a bloated model that fits neither. A [context map](node:Context%20map) records where meanings change and how terms translate between contexts.

Maintaining the language takes ongoing work. Keep a short glossary in the repository, using the words domain experts use. When a discussion changes the meaning of a term, rename the class, the method and the database column as part of the same work, or the code and the conversation drift apart. If a concept is hard to name, raise it with the experts as a modelling question, since the difficulty often means the concept is not yet understood.

The vocabulary feeds the [domain model](node:Domain%20model), where each important term has a corresponding type or method. A developer reading the code and an expert describing the process should then be using the same words for the same things.
quotes: Is a member the person paying or the person on the plan?
Ask support, then use their word everywhere. Right now the code calls both `user`.

nodes.name: Context map
nodes.description: A document or diagram showing a system's bounded contexts and the relationships between them.
nodes.markdown:
A context map is a document or diagram that shows the bounded contexts in a system and the relationships between them. Eric Evans introduced it in Domain-Driven Design (2003). Each relationship records which side depends on which, how their models translate, and how the teams coordinate.

The map makes hidden dependencies visible. Without one, a team renames a field in its event and learns from an incident that three other teams were consuming it. A context map shows who is upstream, whose changes flow to others, and who is downstream and absorbs them. It also shows where one word carries different meanings, so that each context keeps its own [ubiquitous language](node:Ubiquitous%20language).

| Relationship                                          | Meaning                                               |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Partnership                                           | Two teams plan and release dependent changes together |
| [Shared kernel](node:Shared%20kernel)                 | Two contexts jointly own a small shared model         |
| Customer-supplier                                     | Upstream includes downstream's needs in its planning  |
| Conformist                                            | Downstream adopts upstream's model as it is           |
| [Anti-corruption layer](node:Anti-corruption%20layer) | Downstream translates upstream's model into its own   |
| Open host service                                     | Upstream offers a defined protocol for many consumers |
| Published language                                    | Contexts exchange data in a documented shared format  |
| Separate ways                                         | Contexts do not integrate                             |

A map should describe the current situation, including the awkward parts. Drawing the intended architecture hides the problems the exercise is meant to find. If billing is in practice conformist to a vendor's data model, record that, because it shows where a vendor change will land.

The relationships are organisational as well as technical. A customer-supplier arrangement fails if the upstream team has no incentive to serve the downstream team, and [Conway's law](node:Conway's%20law) means team boundaries tend to appear in the integration structure. [Team Topologies](node:Team%20Topologies) offers a related vocabulary for how teams interact.

A context map differs from a container diagram in the [C4 model](node:C4%20model). The C4 diagram shows deployable units and how they communicate. A context map shows model boundaries and team relationships, and one context may span several deployed services. Update it when integrations change.
quotes: Who consumes the `CustomerUpdated` event?
Nobody knows, which is why the last rename broke fulfilment. Let's draw a context map before changing it.

nodes.name: Subdomain
nodes.description: A distinct area of a business's activity, classified as core, supporting or generic to guide investment.
nodes.markdown:
A subdomain is a distinct area of a business's overall activity, such as pricing, billing, shipping or identity. The term comes from Eric Evans's Domain-Driven Design (2003), and it describes the business itself and not the software. An online retailer has these areas whether it runs one application or fifty.

Subdomains are usually classified into three types:

| Type                          | Description                                     | Typical approach             | Retailer example  |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------- |
| [Core](node:Core%20domain)    | Differentiates the business                     | Build in-house, model richly | Pricing           |
| Supporting                    | Specific to the business but not differentiating | Build simply or outsource   | Returns handling  |
| Generic                       | The same problem in most businesses             | Buy or use open source       | Payments, email   |

The classification guides where to spend engineering effort. Without it, teams apply the same level of design everywhere, so an internal admin screen receives an elaborate model while the rules that earn revenue sit in an untested script. Classifying subdomains makes that imbalance visible and supports decisions about what to build, buy or keep simple. A generic subdomain is often best served by a vendor behind a [gateway](node:Gateway%20pattern).

The type depends on the business. Payments is generic for a bookshop and a core domain for a payments company. Classification also changes over time, as a capability that once differentiated a company becomes a commodity available from vendors.

A subdomain differs from a bounded context. The subdomain belongs to the problem space and describes what the business does. A bounded context belongs to the solution space and marks a boundary within which one model and its [ubiquitous language](node:Ubiquitous%20language) apply. Aligning them one to one is a reasonable starting point, but legacy systems often have one context covering several subdomains, and a large subdomain may be split across contexts.

Identify subdomains by asking domain experts what the business does and where the work differs. The existing module structure is a weak guide, because it may reflect history or team layout, as [Conway's law](node:Conway's%20law) predicts.
quotes: Should we write our own invoicing engine?
Invoicing is a generic subdomain for us. Buy one and keep our engineers on pricing.

nodes.name: Core domain
nodes.description: The part of a business that differentiates it from competitors and deserves the most design investment.
nodes.markdown:
A core domain is the part of a business that differentiates it from competitors and that it must do well to succeed. For a logistics company it might be route optimisation, and for an insurer it might be risk pricing. Eric Evans defined the term as part of strategic design in Domain-Driven Design (2003). It is one of three types of [subdomain](node:Subdomain), alongside supporting and generic.

Identifying a core domain directs limited engineering effort. Without that decision, effort tends to follow technical interest: senior engineers build an in-house authentication system or workflow engine, while the pricing rules that win customers stay in an unowned script that nobody wants to change. The result is polished code in areas a vendor could have supplied and fragile code in the area that decides revenue.

The term is easily confused with "important". Payroll is essential and a failure would be serious, but it rarely distinguishes one company from another, so it is usually generic and bought. The test is whether doing it better than competitors would win business.

| Question                                    | If yes                        | If no                          |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Would doing this better win customers?      | Candidate for a core domain   | Supporting or generic          |
| Could a vendor supply it equally well?      | Buy it                        | Consider building it           |
| Do its rules change with business strategy? | Keep in-house, model carefully | A simple implementation may do |

A core domain justifies investment that other areas do not: a rich [domain model](node:Domain%20model), close work with domain experts, a precise [ubiquitous language](node:Ubiquitous%20language) and experienced engineers. Protect it from vendor and legacy models with an [anti-corruption layer](node:Anti-corruption%20layer), so that outside concepts do not shape its design.

Keep the list short, since a company that labels everything as core has made no decision. The classification can also change. A capability that once set a company apart may become a commodity, at which point it should be simplified or replaced with a product.
quotes: Should we spend next quarter rebuilding the notification service?
Notifications are generic for us. Use a vendor and put that time into the pricing engine, which is our core domain.

nodes.name: Shared kernel
nodes.description: A small part of a domain model that two bounded contexts explicitly share and jointly own.
nodes.markdown:
A shared kernel is a small part of a [domain model](node:Domain%20model) that two bounded contexts explicitly share and jointly own. Neither team can change it without agreeing with the other. Eric Evans described it in Domain-Driven Design (2003) as one of the relationships recorded on a [context map](node:Context%20map).

```typescript
// packages/billing-shipping-kernel/index.ts
export type OrderId = string & { readonly brand: "OrderId" };
export type Money = { cents: number; currency: "EUR" | "USD" };
```

The pattern addresses concepts that must stay identical on both sides. If billing and shipping each define `Money` or `OrderId` and the definitions diverge, values passed between them can be silently misread. Sharing a small package keeps the definition in one place, and the compiler catches disagreements.

The cost is [coupling](node:Coupling) between the two teams. Every change requires coordination, and both contexts must build and test against it before it merges. The usual failure is growth. A package named `common` starts with two types and collects customer logic because that is convenient, until a change for one team breaks another team's deployment. At that stage, teams wait on each other's releases, which is one route to a [distributed monolith](node:Distributed%20monolith).

| Relationship                                          | Who owns the model | Coordination | Use when                                |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Shared kernel                                         | Both teams jointly | High         | Teams work closely, concept is identical |
| Customer-supplier                                     | Upstream team      | Medium       | One team depends on another             |
| [Anti-corruption layer](node:Anti-corruption%20layer) | Each side          | Low          | The models differ                       |
| Separate copies                                       | Each side          | None         | The concepts may diverge                |

A shared kernel differs from a general utility library. A utility library has no domain meaning and holds things like string helpers and date formatting. A shared kernel holds business concepts. It also differs from applying [DRY](node:DRY) across contexts: two definitions that look alike may represent different business concepts, and merging them ties together things that should change independently.

Keep the kernel small, give it tests that both teams run in CI, and require a review from each team on changes. If the teams stop coordinating or move to different release cycles, dissolve it and have each context own its copy.
quotes: Shipping's change to `common` broke our billing deploy again.
That package has become a shared kernel nobody agreed to. Cut it down to `Money` and `OrderId` and move the rest back.

nodes.name: Anti-corruption layer
nodes.description: A translation boundary that stops an external or legacy system's model from spreading into a domain's own model.
nodes.markdown:
An anti-corruption layer is a translation boundary that stops the model of an external or legacy system from spreading into a domain's own model. Code on the inside works only with its own concepts, and the layer converts to and from the foreign representation. Eric Evans described it in Domain-Driven Design (2003).

```typescript
type LegacyCustomer = { CUST_NO: string; STAT_CD: "A" | "S" | "X" };

const statuses = { A: "active", S: "suspended", X: "closed" } as const;

function toCustomer(raw: LegacyCustomer): Customer {
  return new Customer(CustomerId.of(raw.CUST_NO), statuses[raw.STAT_CD]);
}
```

The pattern addresses foreign concepts leaking into new code. A team rewrites a service, but because the data comes from a mainframe, the new classes contain fields like `STAT_CD`, the business logic branches on `"X"`, and every developer has to learn what the old codes mean. With a layer in place, the codes exist in one translation module, and the domain sees `suspended` and `closed`.

The layer usually combines a [facade](node:Facade%20pattern) that simplifies the foreign API, [adapters](node:Adapter%20pattern) that fit it to the interfaces the domain expects, and translators that convert data. It may also reconcile differences in behaviour, for example by combining three legacy calls into one domain operation.

| Option                     | Cost                         | Use when                                     |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Conform to upstream model  | Low now, [coupling](node:Coupling) later | The upstream model is good or the area is generic |
| Thin [gateway](node:Gateway%20pattern) | Low              | Stable API, few concepts cross the boundary  |
| Anti-corruption layer      | Higher, with ongoing mapping | The foreign model is poor and the domain matters |

The layer is a maintenance cost, so apply it where the model matters. Protecting a [core domain](node:Core%20domain) from a legacy schema usually justifies the effort. Wrapping a payment provider used in one generic flow usually does not. It is also a common companion to the strangler fig approach, where it lets new code run beside a legacy system during a migration.

An anti-corruption layer differs from a single adapter. An adapter fits one interface to another, often with one-to-one calls. An anti-corruption layer protects a model, and can contain substantial translation logic and many adapters.
quotes: Why does the new billing code check `STAT_CD === "X"`?
It reads the legacy record directly. Add an anti-corruption layer that maps those codes to our `AccountStatus`.

nodes.name: Entity
nodes.description: A domain object defined by a stable identity that persists as its attributes change.
quotes: The merge script kept both copies of the same customer.
It compared objects by reference. Compare by customer ID, since that is what makes them the same entity.

nodes.name: Value object
nodes.description: An immutable domain object defined entirely by its attributes, with no identity of its own.
quotes: The invoice total is off by a cent, and one line is in dollars.
Prices are plain numbers. Introduce a `Money` value object that stores cents and rejects mixed currencies.

nodes.name: Aggregate
nodes.description: A cluster of domain objects changed as one consistent unit through a single root object.
quotes: Two people edited the same order and it went over the credit limit.
Lines are saved independently. Make `Order` the aggregate root and check the limit in `addLine`.

nodes.name: Domain event
nodes.description: An immutable record of something meaningful that happened in a business domain, named in the past tense.
quotes: An analytics timeout failed the checkout again.
Checkout shouldn't know about analytics. Publish `OrderPlaced` and let analytics consume it separately.

nodes.name: Domain service
nodes.description: A stateless domain operation for a business rule that does not belong to a single entity or value object.
nodes.markdown:
A domain service is a stateless operation that expresses a business rule which does not naturally belong to a single [entity](node:Entity) or [value object](node:Value%20object). Eric Evans described it in Domain-Driven Design (2003). It is named in business language and takes domain objects as arguments, such as `DiscountPolicy.priceFor(order, customer, promotions)`.

```typescript
class DiscountPolicy {
  priceFor(order: Order, customer: Customer, promotions: Promotion[]): Money {
    const best = promotions
      .filter((promotion) => promotion.appliesTo(order, customer))
      .map((promotion) => promotion.discountOn(order.total()))
      .reduce((a, b) => (a.greaterThan(b) ? a : b), Money.zero(order.currency));

    return order.total().subtract(best);
  }
}
```

The pattern addresses rules that make any host object awkward. A discount that depends on an order, a customer's tier and the active promotions could go on `Order`, but then `Order` must know about promotions and tiers. Signs of a misplaced method are a long parameter list of other objects, or a method that reads more from its arguments than from `this`, a smell known as [feature envy](node:Feature%20envy). Moving the rule to a domain service keeps each object focused.

A domain service is easily confused with an application service in a [service layer](node:Service%20layer):

| Aspect     | Domain service              | Application service                            |
| ---------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Contains   | Business decisions          | Orchestration of a use case                    |
| Depends on | Domain objects              | Repositories, transactions, gateways           |
| Example    | Calculate the best discount | Load order, apply discount, commit, send email |
