| Level        | Example                                  | Question to ask                         |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Line         | An unexplained `sleep(200)`              | What race does this work around?        |
| Pattern      | A repository wrapping every ORM call     | What does this layer protect us from?   |
| Architecture | Microservices for a team of four         | Which constraint requires this?         |
| Process      | A daily meeting that informs no decision | What would change if we stopped?        |

The mechanism is copying the visible form of a practice without the conditions that made it work. A large company's architecture solves that company's scale and team structure. A [reference architecture](node:Reference%20architecture) can be misused in the same way when adopted whole. Code pasted from a search result or generated by an assistant carries the same risk when it is merged without being read.

Before adopting a practice, state the problem it solves and how you would know it is working. Record the reasoning in a code comment or an [architecture decision record](node:Architecture%20decision%20record), so the next engineer can tell whether it still applies.

Understanding should also come before deletion. An unexplained line may be a genuine workaround for a production incident, so read its history or test without it on a branch first.

Cargo cult programming differs from a [golden hammer](node:Golden%20hammer), where someone may understand a tool well and still overuse it. Following a team convention is also not a cargo cult when the team knows why the convention exists.
quotes: Why is there a `sleep(200)` before every database call?
Someone copied it from the old worker and nobody knows why. Let's find out what it was guarding against before we remove it.

nodes.name: Premature abstraction
nodes.description: Merging code into a shared abstraction before enough real cases show what those cases have in common.
quotes: I need `renderCard` on the invoice page, but it needs another flag.
That would be the fifth flag. Copy the markup for invoices and we'll see what the two have in common.

nodes.name: Inner-platform effect
nodes.description: A system made so configurable that it becomes a poor copy of the platform it runs on.
nodes.markdown:
The inner-platform effect is the tendency of a configurable system to grow into a poor copy of the platform it runs on. A table of generic `entity`, `attribute` and `value` rows rebuilds a database inside a database. A rules engine that gains conditions, variables and loops becomes a programming language with no debugger, tests or version control. The symptoms are a simple report that needs six self-joins, a configuration edit that takes down production and cannot be diffed, and a "no-code" tool that only one engineer can safely change.

| Inner platform                     | What it re-creates   | What is lost                               |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Entity-attribute-value tables      | Database schema      | Types, constraints, indexes, simple queries |
| YAML with conditions and loops     | Programming language | Type checking, debugger, tests             |
| Visual workflow builder            | Application code     | Diffs, code review, rollback               |
| Custom query language over SQL     | SQL                  | Query features, documentation, tooling     |
| Windowing system inside a web page | Browser or OS        | Accessibility, standard keyboard behaviour |

The effect develops through reasonable steps. To avoid a deployment, a team makes a value configurable. A later request needs a condition, and another needs a variable. Eventually the configuration requires an engineer to write it, and that engineer has fewer tools than the host language provided. The original motive is often [speculative generality](node:Speculative%20generality) or a wish to let non-engineers make changes.

Prefer the platform's own features first. Limit configuration to values, and keep logic in code. If the reason for configuration is that deployment is slow, fixing deployment usually removes the need for it.

Some products do need an extension layer. A multi-tenant product where customers define their own fields needs some metadata model, and a [plugin architecture](node:Plugin%20architecture) or the [interpreter pattern](node:Interpreter%20pattern) can suit users outside the team who must extend the system. In those cases, treat the inner platform as a product, with validation, tests, versioning and documentation, and keep its scope deliberately small.
quotes: Can you change the discount rule in the workflow builder?
Nobody can debug it now that it has loops and variables. Let's move this rule back to code and ship it through CI.

nodes.name: Not invented here
nodes.description: Rejecting existing solutions and rebuilding them in-house, mainly because they came from outside the organisation.
nodes.markdown:
Not invented here is the tendency to reject an existing solution and build an in-house replacement, mainly because the solution came from outside the team or organisation. It is recognisable in a company that maintains its own authentication library, date parser, job queue and CSS framework, each with bugs that open-source projects fixed years ago. The engineer who wrote each one has often left, and new hires have to learn tools that exist nowhere else.

Writing the first version is usually a small part of the cost. The team also takes on security patches, documentation, onboarding and edge cases in areas such as time zones, Unicode and cryptography. That effort comes out of work on an organisation's [core domain](node:Core%20domain), the part of the business that sets it apart. Generic [subdomains](node:Subdomain) such as email delivery or payments processing are usually better bought or adopted.

The decision depends on several factors:

| Factor             | Favours adopting                       | Favours building                       |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Business relevance | Generic capability                     | Differentiates the product             |
| Fit                | Meets needs with small adaptations     | Requires heavy workarounds             |
| Risk area          | Security, cryptography, date handling  | Narrow, well-understood logic          |
| Project health     | Actively maintained                    | Abandoned or unmaintained              |
| Dependency size    | Proportionate to what you use          | Large package for one small function   |

The opposite failure is also a risk. Importing a large package for one function adds supply-chain exposure and upgrade work, and a few lines of well-understood code may be the better choice. Building can also be justified by licensing, latency or compliance requirements that no external option meets.

When adopting a dependency, limit how far it spreads. An [adapter](node:Adapter%20pattern) or [anti-corruption layer](node:Anti-corruption%20layer) keeps the vendor's types out of business code, so the dependency can be replaced later. Record the reasoning in an [architecture decision record](node:Architecture%20decision%20record), including what would cause the team to revisit it.
quotes: Our date library has handled daylight saving wrongly again.
We wrote it years ago and nobody owns it. Let's move to a maintained library behind one small wrapper.
